questions.question_text:
Are the lines $y = 5x + 2$ (blue) and $y = 5x - 1$ (red) parallel?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=5.4cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-2,xmax=2,ymin=-8,ymax=8,xtick={-2,-1,0,1,2},ytick={-8,-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6,8},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,blue,<->,domain=-2:1.2,samples=2] {5*x+2};\addplot[thick,red,dashed,<->,domain=-1.4:1.8,samples=2] {5*x-1};\node[blue,left] at (axis cs:1.0,7.4) {$y=5x+2$};\node[red,right] at (axis cs:1.4,6.6) {$y=5x-1$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.text: No, their $y$-intercepts differ, so they are not parallel.
options.why: Judged by the intercepts, but parallelism depends only on the gradients.

options.text: No, one line is steeper than the other.
options.why: Misread the equal coefficients of $x$ as different steepness.

options.text: No, parallel lines must share the same $y$-intercept.
options.why: Confused the intercept with the gradient as the test for parallel lines.

questions.solution_text:
$y=5x+2$ has gradient $5$.
$y=5x-1$ has gradient $5$.
The gradients are equal, so the lines are parallel.

questions.question_text:
Are the lines $y = 4x + 1$ (blue) and $y = 2x + 1$ (red) parallel?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=5.4cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-2,xmax=2,ymin=-7,ymax=9,xtick={-2,-1,0,1,2},ytick={-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6,8},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,blue,<->,domain=-2:1.9,samples=2] {4*x+1};\addplot[thick,red,dashed,<->,domain=-2:2,samples=2] {2*x+1};\node[blue,left] at (axis cs:1.6,7.4) {$y=4x+1$};\node[red,below right] at (axis cs:1.9,4.8) {$y=2x+1$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.text: No, the gradients $4$ and $2$ are different.

options.why: Judged parallelism from the equal intercepts instead of the gradients.
Assumed any two upward-sloping lines are parallel.
Claimed the lines never meet, but different gradients force them to cross.

questions.solution_text:
$y=4x+1$ has gradient $4$.
$y=2x+1$ has gradient $2$.
The gradients are different, so the lines are not parallel.

questions.question_text:
A line is parallel to $y = 3x + 7$.
What is the gradient of that parallel line?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=5.4cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-5,xmax=2,ymin=-4,ymax=10,xtick={-4,-2,0,2},ytick={-4,-2,0,2,4,6,8,10},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,blue,<->,domain=-3.6:0.9,samples=2] {3*x+7};\node[blue,right] at (axis cs:0.3,8.6) {$y=3x+7$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Used the constant term $+7$ instead of the coefficient of $x$.
Negated the gradient, which is the rule for perpendicular, not parallel, lines.
Took the reciprocal of the gradient instead of keeping it equal.

questions.solution_text:
Parallel lines have equal gradients.
$y=3x+7$ has gradient $3$, so any line parallel to it also has gradient $3$.

questions.question_text:
Which two of the lines $y = 4x - 1$ (blue), $y = 2x + 3$ (red) and $y = 4x + 2$ (green) are parallel?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=5.4cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-3,xmax=3,ymin=-8,ymax=9,xtick={-2,0,2},ytick={-8,-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6,8},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,blue,<->,domain=-1.7:2.4,samples=2] {4*x-1};\addplot[thick,red,dotted,<->,domain=-3:2.9,samples=2] {2*x+3};\addplot[thick,green!60!black,dashed,<->,domain=-2.4:1.7,samples=2] {4*x+2};\node[blue,right] at (axis cs:1.9,6.6) {$y=4x-1$};\node[red,below right] at (axis cs:2.4,7.4) {$y=2x+3$};\node[green!60!black,left] at (axis cs:1.2,6.4) {$y=4x+2$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Paired lines with different gradients ($4$ and $2$).
Paired lines with different gradients ($2$ and $4$).
Overlooked that $y=4x-1$ and $y=4x+2$ share gradient $4$.

questions.solution_text:
$y=4x-1$ has gradient $4$.
$y=2x+3$ has gradient $2$.
$y=4x+2$ has gradient $4$.
The two lines with equal gradients are $y=4x-1$ and $y=4x+2$, so these are the parallel pair.

questions.question_text:
Line $A$ passes through $(0,0)$ and $(1,3)$.
Line $B$ passes through $(2,1)$ and $(4,7)$.
Are the lines parallel?
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=5.4cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-1,xmax=5,ymin=-6,ymax=9,xtick={-1,0,1,2,3,4,5},ytick={-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6,8},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,blue,<->,domain=-1:2.9,samples=2] {3*x};\addplot[thick,red,dashed,<->,domain=0.5:4.6,samples=2] {3*x-5};\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=2pt,blue] coordinates {(0,0) (1,3)};\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=2pt,red] coordinates {(2,1) (4,7)};\node[blue,above left] at (axis cs:2.2,7.2) {$A$};\node[red,below right] at (axis cs:3.9,6.4) {$B$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.text: No, the lines pass through different points.
options.why: Judged by the points, not by the equal gradients.
Used the rise $6$ without dividing by the run $2$.
Divided run by rise instead of rise by run for line A.

questions.solution_text:
Gradient of $A=\frac{3-0}{1-0}=3$.
Gradient of $B=\frac{7-1}{4-2}=\frac{6}{2}=3$.
The gradients are equal, so the lines are parallel.
